title: A secret was committed: rotate, purge, force-push

scenario.brief:
**The incident.** A payment API key was committed to `api/src/config.ts` a few commits back. Someone already removed it in a later commit — but that does nothing: the key is still sitting in the git history, readable by anyone who clones the repo. It must be treated as compromised.

Do the real incident drill, in order:

1. **Rotate first.** A key in history is burned. Revoke it at the provider and issue a new one, injected via the environment — never recommit it. (Nothing to validate here; it's the most important step.)
2. **Purge it from history.** Rewrite history so no commit contains the key — `git filter-repo --replace-text` (or the BFG). Every affected commit gets a new id.
3. **Force-push, safely.** History changed, so a normal push is rejected. Push with `--force-with-lease`, which refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime — never a bare `--force`.
4. **Write the incident note.** Open an issue recording what leaked, when, that it was rotated, and the purge.

Tell teammates to re-clone; their old copies still contain the key.
scenario.whyItMatters: Leaked credentials are one of the most common real security incidents. The reflex that matters is the order: rotate first (purging a live key is pointless), then rewrite history, then force-push with lease so you don't clobber a teammate. This is exactly what a calm responder does.

setup: Rotate the key at the provider and set the new one via the environment. Do not recommit it.
Purge the key from history: `git filter-repo --replace-text <(echo 'OLD_KEY==>REMOVED')` (or use the BFG). This rewrites commit ids.
Force-push with a lease: `git push --force-with-lease origin main`. If it's rejected because someone else pushed, fetch and re-run — never use a bare --force.
Open an issue as the incident note (what leaked, when, rotated, purged), and tell the team to re-clone.
Press Check my work once main's history is clean and the force-with-lease push has landed.

objectives.title: The key is gone from the entire history of main
hints: A later 'remove the key' commit is not enough — the key is still in the earlier commit.
Rewrite history with git filter-repo --replace-text (or BFG) so no commit contains it.
Verify with `git log -p | grep` — the key should appear nowhere.

objectives.title: You force-pushed with --force-with-lease
hints: Rewriting history means a normal push is rejected.
Use `git push --force-with-lease origin main`, which refuses if someone else pushed since you fetched.
Never a bare `git push --force` on a shared branch.

objectives.title: Rotated the key and wrote the incident note
hints: Rotation happens at the provider; this is the step that actually stops the leak.
Open an issue recording what leaked, when, that it was rotated, and that history was purged.
Tell teammates to re-clone — their old clones still contain the key.

debrief.summary: You ran a credential-leak incident the professional way: rotated the key first, purged it from the entire git history, force-pushed with a lease, and recorded an incident note.
internals: A commit is immutable, but history is a chain of commits you can rebuild. filter-repo/BFG replays every commit with the secret scrubbed, producing new commit ids for everything from the leak onward.

Because the ids changed, remote history diverged from yours — a normal push is refused. `--force-with-lease` overwrites the remote only if it still matches what you last fetched, so you can't silently clobber a teammate's push.
Rotation is the real fix: anyone who already cloned has the old key, and purging history cannot reach their disks. Purging limits future exposure; rotation stops the leak.
Everyone must re-clone or hard-reset: their local history still contains the secret and the old commit ids.

keyCommands.note: Rewrite history, replacing the secret in every commit.
Publish rewritten history without clobbering others' pushes.
Confirm the secret appears in no commit.

commonMistakes: Just deleting the key in a new commit — it stays in history and is still compromised.
Purging but not rotating — the leaked key is already out; it must be revoked.
Using bare `--force`, which can silently overwrite a teammate's work; use `--force-with-lease`.
Forgetting to tell the team to re-clone, so the secret lives on in their clones.
debrief.atWork: This is a standard security runbook. The ordering — rotate, purge, force-with-lease, communicate — is what separates a contained incident from a prolonged one.
debrief.interview: "A secret got committed. What do you do?" Answer: rotate it immediately (assume compromised), purge it from history with filter-repo/BFG, force-push with lease, and have everyone re-clone.
